citationText: Cary Funk and Kim Parker, “4. Blacks in STEM Jobs Are Especially Concerned About Diversity and Discrimination Conclusion There is no question about the direction the industry is heading when it comes to incorporating AI and machine learning. As this technology improves, newer algorithms are being written and neural networks are being created to “think” more like a human brain. However, it is still a complicated process that relies on humans training the systems to search for specific data sets and modeling of human behavior. And ultimately, M&E is oriented around audiovisual art, which will always have a high level of subjectivity. We will best integrate art with automation by embracing our humanity further. We need to recognize how our human needs, curiosities, and perspectives make workflows better. We must prioritize encouraging people from diverse backgrounds to become workflow professionals so that their unique perspectives can contribute to pushing the M&E industry to be more efficient for all types of people and content. As we continue to learn about and shape these workflows, we need to engage more with experts in AI ethics and data science to further understand possibilities and pitfalls. Until technology can fully replicate human behavior and psychology, humans will always be a necessary part of a workflow. Making sure we address the shortfalls of technology while establishing the best environment for humans to succeed is important. We must also remember the workflow of the past to not fall into the same ethical traps as our predecessors. By having a diverse talent pool, working to combat the biases inherent in AI, and using automation intentionally and thoughtfully, we can create inclusive and efficient workflows to support an industry of authentic storytelling.
